title: The Analytics Edge (Bertsimas, O'Hair, Pulleyblank; Dynamic Ideas 2016): publisher's book page (educational philosophy, distinguishing characteristics)
contribution: The publisher's page of The Analytics Edge, in the three authors' joint first person, states the book's philosophy: real problems come unlabelled; data are "the only objective reality", though possibly incomplete and of questionable quality; problems and data lead and models support, against methods-first books and classes. Chapters start from a real problem and a data set, the methods come last, and the book serves an MIT Sloan class, an Executive MBA class on ten chapters and the edX MOOC 15.071x (p. 1).
problem_entry: DA AP; ML, LO and IO only as tools. The object is "the science of using data to build models, improve decisions, and ultimately add value to institutions and individuals" (p. 1). Entry: real problems "do not come with labels, meaning that they are not necessarily regression problems or optimization problems" (p. 1). The gap named lies in teaching: books and classes "in which methods play the leading role" (p. 1).
key_idea: "Problems and data play a leading role in this book, while models play an essential but supporting role." (p. 1). Chapter template: a real problem from the authors' experience and a data set, then several methods; organization by application area; a methods overview and exercises at the end (p. 1). Kept from methods-first texts: the toolkit (prerequisite "a basic class on regression, probability and optimization"); changed: the order and the table of contents (p. 1; B018 pp. 1-5).
assumptions: Data stance: "The only objective reality is data, which itself may be incomplete and of questionable quality" (p. 1); models serve "to facilitate the solution of real world problems" (p. 1). Materials: data sets for some chapters and for the exercises, an R instruction manual and R script files (p. 1). Audience: MBA, undergraduate and graduate students with the stated prerequisite; the MOOC assumes no background (p. 1). No model class, data set or solver is named beyond the topic list.
experiments: n/a on the page: each chapter is said to show how analytics "has provided an edge", with no measure, baseline or failure (p. 1). Teaching use is reported instead: a one-semester MIT Sloan class; a shorter Executive MBA class on Chapters 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14 and 19; the MOOC 15.071x (p. 1). Mapped onto B018's titles (my mapping): no executive chapter is one whose title or section titles name optimization (5, 12, 21, 22), and kidney allocation (10), revenue management (17) and the emergency-department simulation (18) are left out; no reason is given.
positioning: Set against "the vast majority of books and classes available today" (p. 1); no book or school is named. A parallel in another joint book, not one voice: "Data represent an objective reality; models only exist in our imagination." (B009 p. 1, 2019, with Dunn), without the 2016 qualification; note 02 records the pair as a tension with his robust-optimization view of data [02 C3]. The same stance for the 2004 Data, Models, and Decisions (with Freund): "Rather than covering methodology" (B008 p. 1) [02 P1, T9].
writing: Blurb formula "unified, insightful, modern and entertaining" (p. 1), shared with his other book descriptions (B008 p. 1; B002 p. 1) [02 R15]. Joint first person; impact asserted without numbers. Reading notes, not findings: "often will defined" as printed; "It is structured in seven parts:" followed by eight names, while the printed contents have Parts I-VIII (B018 p. 5) (p. 1).
limits_future: The page states no limits and does not say how an edge is measured. Instructor solutions are released on request through a form, which was not used (p. 1). Not read: the preface (book p. xiii; B018 p. 1) and the chapters.

method_links.note: Method 5's starting point in teaching form: a real problem from the authors' experience, its data, the aim to improve decisions. No decision owner, current rule or decision metric; the edge is asserted, not scored.

[inferred] In the teaching voice the optimization label comes after the problem and the data, as one of several methods. Method 1's exact LP, conic or MIO casting is a research move that the page neither states nor rejects: scope, not contradiction.

title: The Analytics Edge: table of contents (library PDF via B3Kat/BVB)
contribution: The printed contents of The Analytics Edge (pp. vii-xi), read as titles only: seven application parts with 20 chapters (humans and machines, sports and games, healthcare, the internet, crime, operations, finance), then Part VIII on methods and exercises (book pp. 361-446, about a fifth of the text). Every chapter ends with notes and sources; linear and integer optimization get the shortest methods section but 17 of the 51 exercise pages (pp. 1-5).
problem_entry: DA AP; ML, LO, IO and simulation as tools. Seven application parts, then "Methods and Exercises to Put the Analytics Edge into Action" (p. 5). Chapters open on a story, an institution or a question, not on a method: "Models Versus Experts", "How Do You Make a Grandmaster Blink?", "What is Watson?", "Predictive Policing" (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: [inferred from titles and page numbers] Applications first (book pp. 1-360), methods last (book pp. 361-446): the order B017 states (p. 1), carried out in the contents. All 22 chapters close with "Notes and Sources". The methods part lists linear regression, logistic regression, CART and random forests, clustering, data visualization, and linear and integer optimization, and the exercises follow that order; 21.6 "Linear and Integer Optimization" has book pp. 389-390, the shortest methods section, while 22.6-22.7 take 17 of the 51 exercise pages (pp. 1-5).
assumptions: Titles only. Data and institutions named: wine prices, Supreme Court decisions, claims data, the Artemis NICU project, AdWords, Netflix, Amazon, eHarmony, gangs and policing in Chicago, American Airlines, Harrah's Cherokee, the BIDMC emergency department (pp. 1-4). Model classes named: decision trees, the Framingham Risk Score, PageRank, the Condorcet method, a dynamic crime index, centrality, a simulation model, option pricing, alpha models, portfolio construction, integer optimization (pp. 1-5).
proof_devices: Title level: a fast heuristic, an integer-optimization formulation (starred) and results for league structures (5.3-5.5, p. 2)
Title level: a formulated problem (starred), a heuristic for it, and a section assessing the heuristic, "How Good is the Heuristic?" (16.4-16.6, p. 4); the yardstick is not visible
Four starred sections (5.4, 12.5, 16.4, 19.4), three of them formulation or optimization sections; the contents do not say what the star means (pp. 2-5)
experiments: Titles only. Result sections: Results (5.5), The Results (8.3), Numerical Evidence (10.3), How Good is the Heuristic? (16.6), what-if analyses of the simulation model (18.3), Simulation and Performance (20.4). Closing claim sections such as The Competitive Edge of Models (1.4), The Power of Analytics (10.4), The Edge of Simplicity (11.4), The Strength of Simulation (18.4) and Impact (19.5) (pp. 1-5). Baselines, current rules and failures cannot be read from titles.
positioning: [inferred from titles] The book opens with "Models Versus Experts" (ch. 1, p. 1): a model against human judgment, the incumbent. Five chapter topics match his own works by title: ch. 8 and S050; ch. 10 and S044; ch. 17 and S034, S066, S074; ch. 20 and S101; ch. 18 and the 2008 MIT thesis S449 (skipped); this fits B017's "typically from our experience" (B017 p. 1). The 2025 healthcare book reverses the order, foundations first and case studies second (B008 p. 1).
writing: Story and question titles ("Recommendations Worth a Million", "What Burglaries and Earthquakes Have in Common"); dated scenes in the IBM chapters ("February 14, 2011 - The Game is Afoot"); the brand word "Edge" in seven titles (1.4, 4.6, 11.4, 12.3, 13.6, ch. 20, Part VIII) (pp. 1-5).
limits_future: Eight parts, 22 chapters, 136 numbered sections; preface book p. xiii, references book p. 447, index book p. 459 (pp. 1, 5). [inferred from page numbers] Healthcare is the largest application part (book pp. 121-188), operations and finance the smallest; chapters run 12-24 pages. Limits: titles only; the preface is not in the file; no chapter is attributed to an author.

method_links.note: Titles only: decision chapters (allocation policies with numerical evidence, simulation what-if analyses, revenue management, portfolio construction) beside prediction titles in chs. 1, 7, 8, 9 and 15; ch. 1 sets models against experts; baselines and decision metrics are not visible.

Titles only: a fast heuristic and an integer-optimization formulation, with results, in one teaching case (5.3-5.5), and a section judging a heuristic (16.6); the yardstick is not visible and the integer-optimization sections are starred.

Methods are not the organizing unit: one closing methods part, about a fifth of the text, in which linear and integer optimization have the shortest section (book pp. 389-390) [inferred from page numbers].

title: Machine Learning under a Modern Optimization Lens (Bertsimas, Dunn; Dynamic Ideas 2019): publisher's book page (structure, philosophical principles)
contribution: The publisher's page of Machine Learning under a Modern Optimization Lens (with Dunn) gives the seven-part structure (regression, trees, prescriptive ML, optimization over randomization, unsupervised, matrix methods, ML for interpretable optimization), the 2021 Lanchester Prize and six one-line philosophical principles: interpretability matters; practical tractability, not polynomial solvability; NP-hardness as an opportunity; ML linked to optimization, not probability, with data as objective reality; optimization over randomization; prescription, not prediction (p. 1).
problem_entry: ML; IO, CP and RO as engines; DA. Machine learning is framed as a field of optimization: "ML is inherently linked to optimization not probability theory." (p. 1). The parts recast ML tasks one by one, ending with the reverse direction, ML for optimization (p. 1).
key_idea: Six principles (p. 1): "Interpretability is materially important in the realworld."; "Practical tractability not polynomial solvability leads to real world impact."; "NP-hardness is an opportunity not anobstacle."; "ML is inherently linked to optimization not probability theory. Data represent an objective reality; models only exist in our imagination."; "Optimization has a significant edge over randomization."; "The ultimate objective in the real world is prescription,not prediction." [inferred] Kept: the ML task list; changed: the home discipline and the yardstick.
assumptions: Problem classes by part: robust, sparse, nonlinear and holistic regression; optimal classification and regression trees; prescriptive methods; design of experiments, exceptional responders, stable regression and the bootstrap; imputation and clustering; sparse PCA, sparse inverse covariance, factor analysis, matrix and tensor completion (p. 1). Data stance: the second sentence of principle 4 (p. 1), without B017's 2016 qualification. No data set, solver, size or time is named.
experiments: None on the page. The one outside judgment reported is the prize: "This book was awarded the 2021 INFORMS Frederick W. Lanchester Prize" (p. 1).
positioning: Rivals are named by contrast, never by author: probability theory, randomization, polynomial solvability, prediction (p. 1). Part IV "shows the power of optimization over randomization in design of experiments, exceptional responders, stable regression and the bootstrap"; Part VII reverses the lens (p. 1). The same positions in his own papers are carded separately (S178 p. 5; S010 p. 8; S008 p. 29).
writing: One-line principles without evidence or hedging; four of the six are built as a contrast with not (principles 2, 3, 4, 6) (p. 1). Reading notes: run-together words in the page's own HTML ("andextensions", "MLmethods", "inversecovariance", "realworld", "anobstacle", "prescription,not"), checked live on 2026-10-29; NP is in italics there, so the space in note 02's quotation of principle 3 is an extraction artefact. The prize statement stands where the older summary had its paragraph of claims (B010 p. 1) [inferred].
limits_future: The page states no limits: nothing on solver dependence, solve times, certification or losing regimes (the critique record supplies them [05 §1-2]). Principle 4 sits against his own probability work (Tension T3; [02 C4]). The book body and preface were not read.

title: Review of Machine Learning under a Modern Optimization Lens by Thibaut Cuvelier, developpez.com (6 December 2020, in French), with the site's chapter list
contribution: A signed French review (Thibaut Cuvelier, developpez.com, 6 December 2020) of the ML-lens book, with the publisher's older English summary and a third-party list of 26 chapter titles. The reviewer says modern optimization tools let the book replace heuristics by optimal methods, judged on case studies and synthetic data; that the stance is not yet followed by the wider AI community, most content is the authors' own research and most algorithms lack a widespread implementation; and that the book is rigorous yet readable (p. 1). The reviewer's voice is peer critique, not evidence of his methods.
problem_entry: ML; IO and CP as engines. Reviewer: ML algorithms date from decades ago, while "les outils d'optimisation (surtout en nombres entiers et avec des matrices semi-définies positives) ont fait d'énormes progrès" (p. 1). Publisher (older summary): "solutions to central ML problems at large scale that can be found in seconds/minutes, can be certified to be optimal in minutes/hours, and outperform classical heuristic approaches in out-of-sample experiments" (p. 1).
key_idea: Publisher: "an original treatment of machine learning (ML) using convex, robust and mixed integer optimization" (p. 1). Reviewer: methods that bring "des solutions optimales, impossibles à améliorer" in place of heuristics of very variable quality, a stronger reading than the publisher's certified in minutes/hours [my comparison]; each technique from first principles, with the current heuristics and their drawbacks (often interpretability) first (p. 1).
assumptions: Reviewer: case studies against current heuristics and numerical studies on synthetic data (p. 1); prerequisites: a grounding in learning and real optimization skills, convex and integer (p. 1). Third-party chapter list (structure only): 26 titles, from "The Optimization Lenses" to "Interpretable Optimization"; by my mapping trees are the largest group (6 titles), eight titles begin with "Optimal", and the classical CART chapter precedes the optimal-tree chapters (p. 1).
experiments: The reviewer reports the evaluation design but no numbers (p. 1). The practical gap: "il n'existe pas encore d'implémentation répandue pour la plupart des algorithmes présentés" (p. 1).
positioning: Reviewer: "Ce parti pris n'est pas encore suivi par la communauté de l'intelligence artificielle au sens large"; much of the content is the authors' and their collaborators' own research, though the reference list is long and diverse; "Il ne s'agit pas du tout d'un ouvrage de probabilités ou de statistiques" (p. 1). For note 05: the first review of this book on file [05 Gaps]; route the reviewer's points to peer critique (implementation gap: [05 §7.3, §2.7]; headline read at face value: Tension T6; ML Cautions).
writing: Reviewer: "Ils adoptent un style très rigoureux, mais le texte reste lisible"; usable as an advanced optimization text (p. 1). Publisher summary against B009, not merged: the opening paragraph is here (also B008 p. 1) and the prize statement on B009; seven principle lines here, with "Data represent an objective reality; models only exist in our imagination." on its own line, against six bullets on B009; ordinary spacing here, run-together words on B009 (p. 1; B009 p. 1).
limits_future: Reviewer's limits: not yet followed beyond the authors' circle; mostly their own research; few widespread implementations; demanding prerequisites (p. 1). The review gives no numbers, names no competing book and does not report trying code or data.

method_links.note: Voice 1 only (the publisher's older summary, the same paragraph as B008 p. 1), not the reviewer: certified optimal in minutes/hours and better than classical heuristics out of sample, the certificate-and-duel claim as the book's headline; a candidate Stated line. Tension T1 and C9 concern whether the papers deliver it. The reviewer's account of the comparison design is an outside observation for note 05, not counted here.
Voice 1 only: solutions at large scale found in seconds/minutes; practical tractability as the headline, with no speed-up figure.

Reviewer's voice (peer critique, not his methods): the approach is not yet followed by the wider AI community, the content is mostly the authors' own research, and most algorithms lack a widespread implementation (cf. [05 §7.3, §2.7]). The reviewer also reads the optimality headline at face value (Tension T6, inferred).

transferable: (D5) Compare each optimal method with the common heuristic twice, on real case studies and on synthetic data (as the reviewer describes the book, p. 1).
(D8) Release usable implementations with a methods book; the reviewer names their absence as the practical gap (p. 1).
(D7) Introduce each technique from first principles, with the current heuristic and its drawbacks first (as the reviewer describes the book, p. 1).

title: Introduction to Linear Optimization: errata sheet (last updated 7/5/2021), Athena Scientific
contribution: The authors' errata sheet for Introduction to Linear Optimization (with Tsitsiklis), last updated 7/5/2021: 68 items in three lists by printing (13 still listed for the third and later printings, 31 fixed after the second, 24 after the first), from book p. 22 to p. 585. Mostly exercises (23), formula slips (16), typos and names (18), with 8 statement changes, a replaced table, a corrected figure and a figure missing from some copies of the 6th printing (pp. 1-5).
problem_entry: LO; IO in chs. 10-11. What the authors corrected after publication (pp. 1-5). By the chapter page ranges of B004 (pp. 2-5; my mapping), duality (ch. 4, 11 items), sensitivity analysis (ch. 5, 10) and network flows (ch. 7, 12) hold 33 of the 68.
key_idea: Three lists by printing, the first headed "Errata in the third and subsequent printings", the other two listing errata corrected in later printings; the printing is identified on the copyright page; each item gives the book page, line or exercise and a replacement; book p. 218 with Figure 5.3 is reproduced whole, being missing "In some copies of the 6th printing" (pp. 1-5).
assumptions: n/a. My classification of the 68 items: 23 exercise items, 16 formula fixes in the text, 8 statement changes, 1 table (Table 11.1, book p. 506), 1 corrected figure (Figure 1.3, book p. 22), 1 missing figure (book p. 218), 6 names, 12 word-level typos (pp. 1-5).
proof_devices: Added hypotheses: "Assume that ui > 0 for all i." (Ex. 2.3, book p. 76; p. 4); "Assume that di > 0 for all i." (Ex. 7.11, book p. 349; p. 4); nonzero free variables in a nondegenerate primal solution (Ex. 4.12, book p. 190; p. 1)

Direction and strictness: Figure 1.3's strict inequalities made non-strict (book p. 22; p. 1); γ ≥ 0 to γ > 0 (Ex. 5.5(c), book p. 223; p. 4); f(x) ≤ t to f(x) ≥ t in a hint (Ex. 11.9, book p. 525; p. 5); "added to the pivot row" to "added to the zeroth row" (book p. 220; p. 2)

Precision: "converges after a finite number of steps" (Ex. 7.35(c), book p. 355; p. 5); "uncapacitated network flow problem" (book p. 316; p. 4); a bound raised from n to n² (book p. 342; p. 2); Lemma 8.2's space from ℜⁿ to ℜᵐ (book p. 373; p. 3)
Exercise 3.8 replaced: deciding whether a degenerate basic feasible solution is optimal "is essentially as hard as solving a general linear programming problem" (book p. 130; p. 4)
An integer-modelling sentence replaced: a binary variable yi that "can be equal to 1 only if" ai ≤ x ≤ ai+1 "and must be 0 otherwise" (book p. 455, in §10.1 by B004 p. 4; p. 5)
No item reports a wrong theorem or proof; the corrections are local (my reading of the 68 items, pp. 1-5)
experiments: n/a. Dating pattern (my classification): exercises are 18 of the 24 items fixed after the first printing, 1 of the 31 fixed after the second, and 4 of the 13 still listed for the third and later printings; the second list is mostly formula slips, typos and names (11, 8 and 6 of its 31 items) (pp. 1-5). [inferred] Classroom use would surface exercise errors first; the reporters are not named.
